rows.q: animal shelters in Ohio
rows.ask: Which is the strongest fit, and why?
rows.answer:
If "strongest fit" means the clearest evidence of hands-on shelter work, **The Cleveland Animal Protective League** [1] stands out, with **League For Animal Welfare** [3] and **Humane Society Of Delaware County** [2] close behind. The right pick depends on the size and focus you need.

- [1] operates "a 40,000-square-foot animal shelter and resource center in cleveland," brought in 6,952 animals in 2024, and is the lead agency in Cuyahoga County for cruelty investigations. Its revenue was $10,411,587 [1].
- [3] describes itself as a "no-kill animal shelter" for Greater Cincinnati that holds about 80 cats and 40 dogs at any time. It reported 2,118 adoptions in 2024 and also runs a wellness clinic [3].
- [2] runs a managed-intake shelter with capacity for about 122 animals. It received 2,197 animals and adopted out 1,906 in 2024 [2].
- Some filings give less detail. **Cincinnati Animal Care** [6] mentions "temporary shelter" but reports no numbers, and **Angels For Animals Inc** [12] lists only veterinary services, education and adoption.

rows.q: animal shelters in Ohio
rows.ask: Which of these run low-cost spay and neuter programs?
rows.answer:
None of the filings provided call a spay/neuter program "low-cost" or list prices [1]–[15]. These do describe spay/neuter work:

- **League For Animal Welfare** runs a Wellness Clinic serving shelter animals, "other area shelters and rescues and ultimately the community at large," with 1,656 spay/neuter surgeries [3].
- **Wood County Humane Society Inc**'s SNIP program "provides assistance to local animal welfare groups, governmental agencies and pet owners" [14]. **Union County Humane Society** spays/neuters its adopted animals "as well as many for local rescue groups" [15].
- **Animal Adoption Foundation** coordinates spay/neuter programs [5], **Animal Shelter Society Inc** "provides programs promoting spaying and neutering" [8], and **Toledo Animal Shelter Association** has a "mandatory spay/neuter program" [4].
- **Humane Society Of Delaware County** generally spays/neuters adopted animals. It also offers free medical care for senior citizens' pets, but the filing doesn't say whether that includes spay/neuter [2].
- **Stark County Humane Society** passes spay/neuter costs on in adoption fees [10].

rows.q: food banks in rural Appalachia that do workforce training, under $500K
rows.ask: Compare the top 3
rows.answer:
**Morgan-Scott Project** [1] reports the most direct food-plus-job-training activity, **City Of Refuge Pulaski** [2] reports the largest food operation, and **Project Healthy Kids** [3] describes its workforce program as still in development.

- **Food:** [1] gave out 916 food boxes plus a weekly food line averaging 85 families. [2] issued about 250,000 pounds of food and supplies to 10,491 families. [3] provides locally made meals to young children and at-risk seniors through regional central kitchens.
- **Workforce training:** [1] reports job training to 42 individuals. [2] lists job training/placement in its mission, but its program text mentions only interview clothing and coaching. [3] "seeks to develop" a workforce program employing people in recovery.
- **Size:** Revenue is $315,307 [1], $227,813 [2], and $244,061 [3].
- **Setting:** The filings give locations (Deer Lodge, TN [1]; Pulaski, VA [2]; Bridgeport, WV [3]) but don't describe any of them as rural or Appalachian.

rows.q: homeless shelters in Louisville
rows.ask: Which of these actually operate a shelter?
rows.answer:
The filings for **Wayside Christian Mission** [1], **Sweet Evening Breeze** [4], **The Healing Place** [7] and **House of Hope Kentucky** [9] describe running overnight or emergency shelter, while **St. John Center** [3] and **Uniting Partners for Women and Children** [8] describe day shelters.

- **Overnight/emergency:** Wayside runs a 100-person low barrier shelter and emergency shelters for men, women and families, lodging "400 and more persons on a nightly basis" [1]. Sweet Evening Breeze provides "emergency shelter" for LGBTQ+ youth [4]. Healing Place lists "overnight shelters" within its addiction recovery program [7]. House of Hope provides "shelter to homeless women" in rehabilitation [9].
- **Day shelter:** St. John Center's day shelter had 52,776 visits [3]. UP serves women and children [8].
- **Unclear from the filings:** **St. Vincent de Paul** lists "Ozanam Inn," but the details are in Schedule O, which isn't shown [2]. **Jefferson Street Baptist Center**'s program text cuts off at "emergenc…" [12].
- **Not shelters themselves:** **Coalition for the Homeless** coordinates the White Flag program, in which three shelters take part [15]. **Louisville Outreach for the Unsheltered** gives rides to shelter and provides hotel rooms [14].

rows.q: addiction recovery programs in West Virginia

rows.answer:
**FMRS Health Systems** [12] and **Recovery Point Of Hunting** [2] have the highest revenue in these results. FMRS describes a broad range of behavioral health services, while Recovery Point's filing describes only a single addiction recovery focus [2][12].

- **Size:** FMRS reports $18,531,010 revenue, $17,245,064 expenses and $13,132,034 assets [12]. Recovery Point reports $6,437,460 revenue, $5,630,510 expenses and $9,412,484 assets [2].
- **Focus:** FMRS lists a "federally funded" substance abuse assessment and treatment program alongside outpatient, crisis, day treatment and case management services [12]. - **Detail in the filing:** FMRS describes its programs individually [12]. Recovery Point's program text repeats its mission and doesn't say what services it delivers [2].
- **Trade-off:** FMRS fits if you want addiction treatment within wider mental health care [12]. Recovery Point is addiction-focused, but you'd need to look beyond its filing to learn how it operates [2].

rows.q: river and watershed conservation groups in Tennessee
rows.ask: Which do hands-on cleanups or restoration?
rows.answer:
Several filings describe hands-on restoration or cleanup work, most specifically **Harpeth Conservancy** [1], **Cumberland River Compact Inc** [2], **Obed Watershed Community Association** [5], **Keep The Tennessee River Beautiful** [7] and **Tennessee Wildlife Federation Incorporated** [15].

rows.q: mental health counseling for teens in Ohio
rows.ask: Which offer free or sliding-scale counseling?
rows.answer:
**None of the filings say whether counseling is free or offered on a sliding scale.** A few mention cost or affordability:

- **Family Life Counseling & Psychiatric Services** states its mission is "to provide affordable and effective mental health intervention for youth and their families" [4].
- **Wood County Childrens Services Association** says its school-based outpatient service was designed to decrease "barriers related to transportation, cost, and stigma," with funding help from the Wood County ADAMHS board [9].

To confirm fees, payment options or insurance accepted, you'd need to contact these organizations directly.

rows.q: boys and girls clubs in Tennessee
rows.ask: Compare the top 3
rows.answer:
**Boys & Girls Clubs of the Tennessee Valley** [2], **Boys and Girls Club of Middle Tennessee** [1] and **Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater Memphis** [3] share a youth-development focus, but their filings differ in size and in how much detail they give.

- **Middle Tennessee (Nashville)** [1]: Revenue $5,973,375 (2024), expenses $6,461,905, assets $6,650,426 (2023). It reports serving "over 4,800 young people" through after-school, summer enrichment and digital programming, built around academic success, healthy lifestyles, and character & leadership.
- **Tennessee Valley (Knoxville)** [2]: Revenue $15,638,309 (2025), expenses $13,378,798, assets $25,401,616 (2023). It has similar priority outcomes. It says most clubs run 21st Century Community Learning Center grants and cites teacher reports of fewer homework mistakes. The excerpt gives no count of youth served.
- **Greater Memphis** [3]: Revenue $8,404,775 (2024), expenses $7,049,599, assets $26,290,567 (2023). It reports about 7,800 youth served in 2024, but its program description is brief ("maintaining facilities and administering various programs").
- **Trade-off:** The Tennessee Valley filing gives the most outcome evidence [2], the Memphis filing gives the highest number served but the least program detail [3], and the Middle Tennessee filing falls in between [1].

rows.q: disaster relief after floods in eastern Kentucky
rows.ask: Which responded to the 2022 floods?
rows.answer:
Only two filings explicitly mention the 2022 floods: **United Helping Hands Of Pikeville Inc** [2] and **Wayland Historical Society Inc** [8].

- **United Helping Hands** set up its Pike County relief services program "specifically to help those affected by flooding that occurred in 2022," and says later flooding has kept it "vital to the region" [2].
- **Wayland Historical Society** says it "helped with federally declared flood disaster in July of 2022" [8].
- Others describe flood work without saying which floods. **East Kentucky Dream Center Inc** helps families "recover from damages related to flooding" [1]. **John Hobson Ministries Inc** offers "assistance for flood relief" [11]. **Coc Benevolent Fund Inc** covers "tornado and flooding" damages [10]. **Florence Lions Clubs Charities Inc** aided "victims of the flooding disaster that occurred during this year" [14]. **Krypton Fire And Rescue** lists "flood rescuse" in its mission [5].
- Their filings don't say whether these efforts included the 2022 floods [1][5][10][11][14].

rows.answer:

rows.q: churches that run food pantries in Tennessee
rows.ask: Which pantries say how many families they serve?
rows.answer:
**Regional Educational And Environ- Mental Program** is the clearest match: it says 750 families received food from its pantry [2]. Two others give family counts for food help but don't tie them specifically to a pantry [9][10].

- **Brinkley Heights Ministries Inc** lists "Food: 1526 Families, 3,955 People" [9].
- **Feed America First Of Tennessee** estimates its food reached about 40,000 families monthly, distributed through partner agencies rather than its own pantry [10].
- These report people rather than families: **Of One Accord Inc** served 41,372 individuals through three food pantries [3], and **Branch Of Nashville Inc** served 16,047 unique people [12].
- **Neighborhood Christian Centers Inc** reports emergency aid, including food, for more than 25,180 individuals, but no count for its mobile pantry alone [11].
- **Solomons Porch Inc** [1], **Helping Hands Of Humphreys County Inc** [5], **Well Outreach** [6] and **Bethesda Community Mission** [7] mention pantries but give no family or person counts.
